content.title: About
content.content: Bay leaves are the leaves of the bay laurel (Laurus nobilis), an evergreen tree native to the Mediterranean. They have a spicy, slightly bitter aroma with notes of mint, pine, and clove. In cooking, dried leaves are usually used, added to soups, meat dishes, sauces, and marinades and removed before serving.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: In ancient Greece and Rome, wreaths of laurel branches were made for victors.
Dried leaves are more aromatic than fresh ones, and their aroma develops during long cooking.
The leaves stay tough even after cooking, which is why they are removed from the dish.
Indian bay leaf (tej patta) is a different plant with a flavor resembling cinnamon.
Cherry laurel and oleander have similar-looking leaves but are poisonous.

items.title: Contains essential oils
items.content: The aromatic compounds in bay leaf, such as cineole, give it its distinctive smell.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: The leaves contain polyphenols with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Adds flavor without extra salt
items.content: The aromatic leaf makes dishes richer without adding salt or calories.

items.title: Traditionally used for digestion
items.content: In folk practice, bay leaf tea is used for stomach discomfort, but there is little scientific evidence.

items.title: Contains small amounts of minerals
items.content: The leaves contain calcium, iron, and manganese, but the amounts in a dish are small.

items.title: Should not be eaten whole
items.content: The tough leaves are hard to chew and can get stuck in the throat or injure the intestines, so they should be removed from the dish.

items.title: Poisonous look-alikes
items.content: Cherry laurel and oleander leaves are poisonous; use only true bay laurel from a reliable source.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Allergic reactions and contact dermatitis are possible.

items.title: Essential oil
items.content: Bay essential oil should not be taken internally.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add one or two dried leaves to soup, borscht, broth, braised meat, rice, sauces, and marinades at the start of cooking, and always remove them before serving. For a stronger aroma, lightly crack the leaf.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried leaves in an airtight jar in a dry, dark place. The aroma fades over time, so use them within a year or two. Fresh leaves can be kept in the refrigerator or dried.

content.title: About
content.content: Cereal O's, NFS is a ready‑to‑eat breakfast made from whole grain wheat, corn and oats, fortified with vitamins and minerals. The flakes have a light crunchy texture and a mildly sweet taste, perfect for a quick breakfast with milk or yogurt.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The product was launched in 2023 as part of the "New Functional Snacks" (NFS) line.
The flakes contain whole grains, not just extracts, preserving more dietary fiber.
Vitamin D is added, a nutrient often missing in typical breakfasts.
Packaging is made from recyclable plastic, reducing environmental impact.
The iconic "O's" shape was inspired by a ring symbolizing an endless energy cycle.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Whole grains provide dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion and satiety.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2 and B6 aid energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron is essential for oxygen transport in the blood and helps prevent fatigue.

items.title: Fortified with vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D enhances calcium absorption and supports bone health.

items.title: Low sugar content
items.content: Sugar is limited to 5 g per 100 g, making it suitable for moderate consumption.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The product contains wheat, so it is not suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although low, individuals monitoring glycemic intake should account for the sugar present.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: A single serving (30 g) provides about 120 kcal; adding milk or yogurt increases total calories.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pour milk, kefir, or a plant‑based drink over the flakes and wait 2–3 minutes. They can also be blended into smoothies, mixed with yogurt, used in baking, or as a crunchy topping for fruit salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, reseal the bag tightly to maintain crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Clams are marine bivalve mollusks that are often prepared fried. Fried clams have tender meat, a slightly sweet flavor, and a crisp crust. They are commonly served as an appetizer or as a component of Asian and Mediterranean dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Clams filter water, helping to clean it of microscopic particles.
In the wild clams can live up to 20 years, but culinary use usually involves younger specimens.
Frying clams is often done with oil, garlic, ginger, or spices to enhance aroma.
Clams are rich in iron and vitamin B12, making them valuable for pescatarians.
In some countries clams are considered a delicacy and are served in high‑end restaurants.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Clams provide complete protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Iron source
items.content: The iron in clams is highly bioavailable and supports hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for nervous system function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Clams contain EPA and DHA, which promote heart and vascular health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Clams supply zinc, selenium and magnesium, contributing to immunity and metabolism.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to clams, ranging from skin rash to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Toxin contamination
items.content: Clams can accumulate toxins and heavy metals from polluted waters; purchase from reputable sources.

items.title: Food poisoning
items.content: Undercooked clams may harbor pathogenic bacteria that cause gastroenteritis.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: When served with soy sauce or added salt, clams can become a source of excess sodium.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fried clams are served hot, often with a dipping sauce made from soy sauce, lemon juice, or spicy chili. They can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, added to salads, noodles, or rice dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh clams in the refrigerator in a sealed container for no more than 1‑2 days. Fried clams are best consumed within 24 hours; if needed, store them in an airtight container in the fridge.

content.title: About
content.content: Gizzard is the edible stomach of birds, most commonly chicken or duck. It has a dense, slightly springy texture and a neutral flavor that readily absorbs seasonings during cooking. Gizzards are widely used in many cuisines as an ingredient for pâtés, stuffing, soups, and fried dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Gizzards are often called “bird meat” because they are high in protein and have a meat‑like texture.
Traditional cuisines of many countries (e.g., China, France, and the United States) feature gizzards in pâtés, stuffed dishes, and sauces.
Gizzards can act as a natural gelling agent thanks to their high collagen content.
In some cultures gizzards are considered a delicacy and appear in special dishes such as French “foie gras de volaille.”
Gizzards are frequently sold frozen or canned, which makes storage convenient.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Gizzards provide about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of collagen
items.content: High collagen content promotes healthy skin, joints, and connective tissue.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many meat products, gizzards contain relatively little fat, especially when visible fat is trimmed.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals are important for blood formation and immune function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Gizzards are a good source of B2, B3, and B12 vitamins, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Gizzards can be contaminated with Salmonella or Campylobacter, so they must be cooked thoroughly.

items.title: Bird allergy
items.content: People allergic to poultry (eggs, chicken meat) may react to gizzards.

items.title: High cholesterol content
items.content: Gizzards contain a notable amount of cholesterol, so individuals with hypercholesterolemia should limit intake.

items.title: Large portions may cause heaviness
items.content: Because of their dense texture, big servings can be hard to digest.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Gizzards are usually cleaned, rinsed, and boiled until tender (about 45 minutes). They can then be minced into pâté, added to ground meat, used in soups, or sautéed with vegetables. Excess fat and membranes are often trimmed before cooking. Serve hot, often with sauces, herbs, or spices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh gizzards in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C for no more than 2 days. Frozen gizzards keep up to 6 months in the freezer. After thawing, use them promptly and do not refreeze. Canned gizzards should be kept in a cool, dry place until the expiration date.

content.title: About
content.content: Horchata is a traditional refreshing drink made from milk, rice, cinnamon and sugar. The milk‑based version gives the beverage a creamy texture and a gentle milky flavor while preserving the characteristic cinnamon aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Horchata originates from Mexico, where it is traditionally prepared with rice, almonds or tiger nuts.
Milk‑based horchata is often served chilled in hot weather as a cooling beverage.
Cinnamon and vanilla are classic flavorings, sometimes complemented with nutmeg.
In some regions coconut milk replaces cow’s milk, creating a tropical twist.
Horchata can be sweet or mildly spiced depending on the amount of sugar and spices used.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: The milk used in the recipe is rich in calcium, which supports bone and tooth health.

items.title: B‑vitamin content
items.content: Rice and milk provide B1, B2 and B12 vitamins important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Probiotic potential (when fermented)
items.content: If the horchata is fermented, beneficial bacteria develop, promoting gut health.

items.title: Low fat (when using skim milk)
items.content: Using skim milk makes the drink lower in calories while still providing protein.

items.title: Antioxidant effect of cinnamon
items.content: Cinnamon contains polyphenols that may help reduce oxidative stress.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort after drinking milk‑based horchata.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Traditional recipes contain a notable amount of sugar, which can increase calorie intake and affect blood glucose levels.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to milk proteins should avoid this beverage.

items.title: Excessive cinnamon
items.content: Large amounts of cinnamon may irritate the stomach in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Horchata can be enjoyed cold as a refreshing drink, paired with desserts, or used in cocktails. It can also be warmed and added to porridge or oatmeal for a creamy flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store prepared horchata in the refrigerator in a sealed container for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑sized containers.
